Q: Why does cpp execute 2 different implementations of the same functions based on the ability to evaluate the result in compile-time? A:

std::ranges::find uses pointer comparison (==) for const char* in both cases.

The reason the first one works is string literal pooling. When you write --runtime twice in your code, the compiler stores them at the same memory address. So args[2] and the literal you're searching for point to the same location, and == returns true.

With getenv(), you get a pointer to a completely different memory location. The content is the same, but the address isn't, so pointer comparison fails. Just use std::string_view instead. Then, == compares the actual characters, not the pointers. Hope you get it.

Q: How to use inverse scaling on React Native apps A:

You should not inverse-scale fonts by screen width/height. The difference you're seeing is caused by device pixel density, font scaling, and platform typography defaults, not screen size.

Spotify achieves consistency by using density-independent units and controlled font scaling, not inverse scaling. Take a look at react-native-size-matters, I believe it could be helpful for what you're trying to achieve as it helps by providing controlled and relative scaling.

So instead of fully scaling fonts up on large fonts, it dampens the scaling and keeps fonts closer to the original design size which may assist with the consistency you're looking for.

Q: Should resume skills be stored as JSON, BLOB, or normalized tables for analytics and search performance? A:

Use a normalized design to support the greatest variety of queries, all with adequate performance and better data integrity. Add indexes to improve specific queries.

Use a denormalized design to improve optimization for one query, at the expense of making other queries worse. This requires that you know all the specific queries you will run, and which one you want to give the highest priority.

Your post has shown a table definition (thank you), but no specific queries. So I agree with the other answer that no one can guess at which design is best for your case.

I agree with the other answer that I'd use a normalized design by default.

I wrote more about optimization, denormalization, and JSON in SQL databases in my book More SQL Antipatterns.

Q: Insert if doesn't exist - in python+sqlalchemy A:

It is possible to do it one call. It wasn't easy because insert.values(**items) doesn't allow a where clause combined with NOT EXISTS. We need a subquery but then we also need literals for every column and the keys for the insert.Also the literal for datetime caused a insert issue (formatting, maybe just postgres). I am wondering if there is a better way for the date issue.

In below example item_dict is a dictionary with field: value entries. It is only inserted if the invoice_number AND invoice_line_number don't already exist.

    # Create literals for select. Datetime conversion was needed because insert failed without it due to formatting issues.
    literals = [literal(val) if key != 'invoice_date' else literal(val.strftime("%Y-%m-%d")) for key,val in item_dict.items() ]
    
    # NOT exists subquery providing the literals.
    insert_select = select(literals).where(
        ~exists(literal(1)).where(
            (performance_row_table.c.invoice_number == item_dict['invoice_number']) &
            (performance_row_table.c.invoice_line_number == item_dict['invoice_line_number'])
        )
    )

    keys = [key for key in item_dict.keys()]
    # Insert using the subquery
    insert_statement = performance_row_table.insert().from_select(keys, insert_select).returning(performance_row_table)

    compiled = insert_statement.compile(compile_kwargs={"literal_binds": True})
    print(compiled)
    insert_result = session.execute(insert_statement).fetchone()
